notes: Statutory demand and chief constable judgment debt; Nicholls' equitable assignment analysis rejected on injustice point.

enrichment.short_title: Coulter v Dorset Police: statutory demand and chief constable judgment debt
key_facts: Mr Coulter owed costs of £6,627.47 under a 1997 judgment obtained by Chief Constable Aldous after Coulter's claim over a stolen car failed.
A statutory demand was served in July 2003 on behalf of the present chief constable, Mrs Stichbury, before any section 136 assignment from Mr Aldous.
The office of chief constable is not a corporation sole; the debt was held for the Dorset police authority and police fund.
Coulter argued the demand was defective and that he had cross-claims arising from Dorset Police's cybersquatting complaint to ICANN.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal from a High Court refusal to set aside a statutory demand in bankruptcy proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the statutory demand should not have been set aside; a bankruptcy petition may be presented after the statutory compliance period.
enrichment.ratio: Where a chief constable holds a judgment debt for the police authority, equitable assignment to a successor on retirement may suffice, but even if the demand was technically defective no injustice required setting it aside once the creditor at the hearing was entitled to the debt and the debtor could pay.
legal_issues: Whether the present chief constable was the creditor when the statutory demand was served
Whether equitable assignment occurred on retirement of the former chief constable
Whether a defective statutory demand must be set aside where the creditor at hearing can pursue bankruptcy
Whether cross-claims for malicious prosecution or misfeasance justified setting aside the demand
linked_authorities: In re a Debtor (No 1 of 1987) [1989] 1 WLR 271

confidence.notes: Central statutory demand issue and appellate disposition are clearly reasoned though the equitable assignment analysis differed from the High Court.

notes: Benefit fraud case stated; perversity and costs discussion on single-judge listing are detailed.

enrichment.short_title: Hastings Council v Jones: false benefit statement and perversity appeal
key_facts: Mrs Jones faced six summonses alleging she knowingly made false statements on housing and council tax benefit applications by failing to declare NHS Trust employment.
She said a friend's advice led her to believe she need only declare employment with CCS Ltd.
Magistrates acquitted her, finding she did not know the statements were false.
Hastings Borough Council appealed by case stated on perversity grounds.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from magistrates' acquittal, heard by a single High Court judge.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the acquittal was reasonably open on the evidence; Council ordered to pay Mrs Jones's costs of the appeal.
enrichment.ratio: On a prosecutor's case stated appeal the question is whether the acquittal was perverse; if the defendant might have believed advice that she was not required to disclose a second job, she lacked knowledge that her statement was false for section 112(1).
legal_issues: Whether Mrs Jones knew her benefit applications were false
Whether the magistrates' acquittal was perverse on the evidence
Effect of third-party advice on knowledge for section 112(1)
Whether inter partes costs could be ordered against a publicly funded successful defendant
linked_authorities: Harrison v Department of Social Security (CO/1244/96)

confidence.notes: Legal issue and dismissal are clear; extended costs discussion is ancillary to the merits.

notes: Landmark blood specimen reasonable excuse case extending Teape and Furby to blood samples.

enrichment.short_title: Martiner: failure to provide blood specimen and undisclosed needle phobia
key_facts: Mr Martiner failed a roadside breath test and was required at Belgravia Police Station to provide a blood specimen after the evidential breath machine was unreliable.
He refused twice, saying it was his human right to say no, without telling the custody sergeant of his needle phobia.
Medical evidence showed moderate needle phobia and Anxious Avoidant Personality Disorder.
The district judge convicted him, finding no causative link between his condition and the deliberate refusal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from a magistrates' court conviction for failing without reasonable excuse to provide a specimen under section 7(6).
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; a motorist who deliberately fails to provide blood without mentioning a known medical condition has no reasonable excuse; conviction upheld.
enrichment.ratio: The duty to inform the constable of a medical condition preventing a breath specimen under Teape v Godfrey applies equally to deliberate failures to provide blood or urine under section 7(6); without disclosure the police cannot seek alternatives and no reasonable excuse arises.
legal_issues: Whether a suspect must inform police of a medical reason for inability to provide a specimen
Whether Teape v Godfrey applies to blood and urine specimens as well as breath
Whether needle phobia provided a reasonable excuse when not disclosed
Whether there was a causative link between the medical condition and the refusal

confidence.notes: First-instance precedent on blood specimens; reasoning and answers to stated questions are explicit.

notes: Boundary wedge trespass appeal; easement of necessity point refused as late and misconceived.

enrichment.short_title: Clements v Goodacre: boundary wedge and 1973 fence agreement
key_facts: A disputed 'wedge' strip separated Greenwood Farm (Clements) and Glendale Manor (Bush) on the boundary with Mr Goodacre's lozenge-shaped land in Heathfield.
In 1973 Mr Goodacre erected a post-and-rail fence with agreement of the then Glendale owner, defining the Lewis boundary.
The judge held the wedge belonged to Clements, not Goodacre, and that Goodacre trespassed when excavating and moving the fence.
Goodacre argued a 1990 bank possession order and registered OS boundaries created issue estoppel excluding the wedge from Clements' title.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Court of Appeal from a county court judgment on boundary ownership and trespass after permission on res judicata/issue estoppel grounds.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the wedge is part of Clements' land; application to raise easement of necessity refused; costs summarily assessed against Goodacre.
enrichment.ratio: Registered general boundaries do not fix title lines; a 1973 boundary agreement showing adjoining holdings abut at the fence is decisive unless objective evidence shows a separate access strip was reserved, which was not established on the facts.
legal_issues: Whether the wedge belonged to Goodacre or Clements/Bush
Whether a 1990 possession order created issue estoppel on boundaries
Effect of Ordnance Survey registered boundaries versus the Lewis fence agreement
Whether an easement of necessity arose over the wedge for the lozenge
linked_authorities: Union Lighterage Co v London Graving Dock Co [1902] 2 Ch 557

confidence.notes: Boundary findings and dismissal are clear; easement point was refused without full merits analysis.

notes: EU enlargement A-8 transitional jobseeker's allowance challenge; Collins ECJ cited but derogation upheld.

enrichment.short_title: D v DWP: A-8 accession jobseeker's allowance and worker registration
key_facts: The applicant is a Latvian national who claimed asylum in 2002; his claim failed but he remained in the UK.
After Latvia's EU accession on 1 May 2004 he challenged domestic regulations restricting A-8 workers' access to Jobseeker's Allowance and imposing worker registration.
Transitional Annex V provisions permitted national measures limiting labour market access for up to five years.
He later obtained employment but the challenge covered both the job-seeking and employed periods.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to apply for judicial review after refusal by Mr Justice Collins.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused with costs; the 2004 Regulations were a permissible derogation from EU free movement and equal treatment rules during the transitional period.
enrichment.ratio: Annex V transitional provisions permit discrimination in access to the labour market including financial benefits facilitating job search; Article 7.2 of Regulation 1612/68 applies only once a person is a worker, and Article 12 does not override the special accession derogation.
legal_issues: Whether A-8 nationals could claim Jobseeker's Allowance while seeking work after accession
Compatibility of habitual residence and worker registration Regulations with EU law
Application of Collins v Secretary of State for Work and Pensions to job-seekers
Whether registration fees and conditions unlawfully discriminated after employment was obtained
linked_authorities: Collins v Secretary of State for Work and Pensions (ECJ) C-138/02

confidence.notes: EU and domestic regulatory framework and refusal of permission are comprehensively reasoned.

notes: Important Part VI Housing Act shared residence order allocation case; decision quashed on flawed household analysis.

enrichment.short_title: Bibi v Camden: housing allocation and 50/50 joint residence order
key_facts: Ms Bibi and her ex-husband Mr Rahman held a joint Camden tenancy; after divorce he obtained three-bedroom re-housing claiming sole care of the children.
A consent joint residence order required the two children to alternate weekly between parents in a true 50/50 arrangement.
Camden's Exceptions Panel offered Ms Bibi only one-bedroom accommodation, saying the children were adequately housed with their father.
The council cited housing shortage and under-occupation if both parents received family-sized homes.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of Camden's housing allocation decision under Part VI of the Housing Act 1996.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded; the allocation decision was quashed for failing properly to assess whether the children were part of the claimant's household under the bedroom standard; matter remitted.
enrichment.ratio: A section 8 residence order is a material but not determinative factor under Part VI; a housing authority must assess the applicant's own household and bedroom needs, not treat another parent's allocation or stock shortage as automatically excluding children from the applicant's household.
legal_issues: Whether a 50/50 joint residence order required three-bedroom allocation to both parents
Application of the bedroom standard and Allocation Scheme to shared residence cases
Whether housing shortage and under-occupation could displace the allocation scheme
Interaction between Family Court residence orders and Part VI housing allocation
index_terms: R v Oxford CC ex p Doyle
R v Port Talbot BC ex p McCarthy
linked_authorities: R v Oxford City Council ex p Doyle [1997] 30 HLR 506
R v Port Talbot Borough Council ex p McCarthy [1990] 23 HLR 203

confidence.notes: Detailed statutory analysis, quashing order and guidance on Family Court interaction are clearly set out.

notes: Complex ICE clause 66 engineer decision and section 67 jurisdiction challenge on Thelwall Viaduct works.

enrichment.short_title: AMEC v SoS Transport: arbitrator jurisdiction and ICE clause 66 decision
key_facts: AMEC carried out renovation works to Thelwall Viaduct on the M6 under ICE 5th edition conditions with Pell Frischmann as engineer.
Disputes over viaduct defects led to engineer decisions under clause 66 and a December 2002 notice of arbitration by the Secretary of State.
AMEC challenged the arbitrator's jurisdiction under section 67 on dispute crystallisation, natural justice and scope of the engineer's decision.
Very large sums were at stake and parallel court proceedings ran against other defendants.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 67 application to the Technology and Construction Court challenging arbitrator jurisdiction after an interim award; permission to appeal granted.
enrichment.outcome: All three jurisdiction challenges rejected; interim arbitral award confirmed under section 67(3)(a); permission granted to AMEC to appeal to the Court of Appeal.
enrichment.ratio: A dispute existed for clause 66 purposes, Pell Frischmann's December 2002 document was a valid engineer decision, and the arbitrator's jurisdiction was not limited to defects A, B and C only; the court reached the same conclusions as the arbitrator on a complete rehearing.
legal_issues: Whether a crystallised dispute existed on 11 December 2002 for arbitration
Whether the engineer's 18 December 2002 decision was valid under clause 66
Whether natural justice rules applied to the engineer's decision-making
Whether arbitrator jurisdiction was confined to specific identified defects

confidence.notes: Main jurisdiction conclusions are explicit though the lengthy judgment covers many procedural sub-issues.

notes: CCRC reference; ADHD diagnosis led to quashing murder conviction and no retrial after eight years custody.

enrichment.short_title: R v Friend: CCRC reference, ADHD and section 35 adverse inference

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994

key_facts: Billy Joe Friend was convicted of murder at 15 for joint enterprise in his brother Ned's fatal stabbing of Ben O'Connor in 1995.
At trial Dr Gudjonsson said he had moderate mental handicap; the judge allowed adverse inference under section 35 from failure to give evidence.
Fresh CCRC evidence diagnosed childhood ADHD unrecognised at trial; Dr Young concluded trial participation and giving evidence were undesirable.
Friend had served over eight years; the Crown conceded no retrial was in the public interest.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second appeal on CCRC reference under section 9 of the Criminal Appeal Act 1995 against a 1996 murder conviction previously dismissed on appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; conviction quashed as unsafe; no retrial ordered; defendant's costs order for pre-CCRC work.
enrichment.ratio: Undiagnosed ADHD and associated cognitive deficits making it undesirable for a young defendant to give evidence, if not available at trial, can render a conviction unsafe where section 35 adverse inference and Lucas lie directions would have differed materially.
legal_issues: Whether section 35 adverse inference should have been drawn given mental condition
Admissibility and effect of fresh psychiatric evidence on trial fairness
Whether the appellant could effectively participate in trial under Article 6
Whether interview evidence and Lucas lie directions were affected by ADHD
linked_authorities: V v United Kingdom [2000] All ER 1024

confidence.notes: Fresh expert evidence, Crown concessions and quashing without retrial are clearly recorded.

notes: Planning section 288 challenge; Inspector's precedent reasoning on Serpentine Green mezzanine upheld.

enrichment.short_title: Next v SoS: mezzanine extension precedent at Serpentine Green centre
key_facts: Next sought planning permission for a 1,000 sq m mezzanine floor at its Serpentine Green store in Peterborough, nearly doubling net sales area.
The shopping centre was capped at 26,000 sq m gross under Policy S5; Tesco Extra occupied about half the centre.
The Inspector refused permission fearing precedent for similar mezzanine extensions in about thirteen smaller units cumulatively harming the city centre.
Two smaller mezzanine permissions had already been granted without significant planning objection.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 288 challenge to an inspector's decision dismissing Next's appeal and refusing planning permission.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; Inspector's reasoning on precedent and cumulative retail floor space impact was adequate; costs summarily assessed at £5,984.
enrichment.ratio: Precedent may be a material planning consideration where granting one relatively small mezzanine would make refusal of similar proposals difficult, producing incremental cumulative floor space increases threatening the city centre retail hierarchy despite each application being decided on its merits.
legal_issues: Adequacy of Inspector's reasons on precedent and cumulative effect
Whether each mezzanine application must be considered only on individual merits at the time
Application of Policy S5 floor space cap and emerging Policy R1 qualitative criteria
Whether smaller prior permissions undermined the precedent argument
linked_authorities: South Buckinghamshire District Council v Porter (No 2) [2004] UKHL 33

confidence.notes: Challenge confined to adequacy of reasons; dismissal and costs are clear though planning merits were not re-argued.

notes: AG reference for unduly lenient manslaughter sentence on vulnerable elderly victim; sentence increased.

enrichment.short_title: AG Ref No 64/2004: unduly lenient manslaughter of elderly victim
key_facts: A 41-year-old woman pleaded guilty to manslaughter on the basis of lack of intent after attacking 68-year-old alcoholic Mr Hyde in his flat.
While drunk and enraged she threw a television, repeatedly stabbed him with a wooden door prop and threw other objects; he died from abdominal injuries.
Mr Hyde had prior sexual offence convictions; the offender attacked him believing he was a paedophile.
She was sentenced to two-and-a-half years' imprisonment on a plea accepted about a month before trial.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference under section 36 of the Criminal Justice Act 1988 alleging an unduly lenient manslaughter sentence.
enrichment.outcome: Reference upheld; sentence quashed and replaced with three-and-a-half years' imprisonment, having regard to double jeopardy and progress in custody.
enrichment.ratio: A sustained violent attack with a weapon on a vulnerable elderly victim causing death warrants a substantially longer sentence than two-and-a-half years; mitigation including family circumstances and remorse did not adequately reflect gravity and public concern about loss of life.
legal_issues: Whether two-and-a-half years was unduly lenient for manslaughter by sustained assault
Weight of aggravating features including victim vulnerability and use of a weapon
Appropriate increase having regard to double jeopardy and mitigation
Sentencing guidance for manslaughter where death results from violent assault
linked_authorities: Attorney-General's References Nos 19, 20 and 21 of 2001 [2002] 1 Cr App R(S) 136

confidence.notes: Facts, aggravating and mitigating features and revised sentence are all clearly stated.
